bio.en: Ada Chen Rekhi is an executive coach and co-founder of the note-taking product Notejoy, formerly SVP of Marketing at SurveyMonkey and an early LinkedIn marketing leader, who helps founders scale themselves.
bio.zh: Ada Chen Rekhi 是一位高管教练，也是笔记产品 Notejoy 的联合创始人，曾任 SurveyMonkey 营销高级副总裁及 LinkedIn 早期营销负责人，专注于帮助创始人实现自我成长。

summary.en: Ada shares a framework called Curiosity Loops for making better decisions by systematically gathering structured input from your network. She walks through a live exercise mapping Lenny's personal values and offers practical advice for intentionally building an early-career path. The conversation also covers how to thrive as a woman in Silicon Valley, when to get a coach versus doing it yourself, and why aligning work with your values prevents a mid-to-late-career trap.
summary.zh: Ada 介绍了她称为“好奇心循环”（Curiosity Loops）的框架，通过向人脉系统性地收集结构化反馈来做出更好的决策。她现场带领 Lenny 梳理个人价值观，并给出如何有意识地规划早期职业路径的实用建议。对话还涵盖女性如何在硅谷茁壮成长、何时该请教练还是自己来，以及为什么让工作与价值观保持一致能避免中年职业困境。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: It's a terrible outcome to wake up one day and be late career and feel trapped because you have a certain lifestyle or a certain expectations of the people around you that you have to go work this job, but then you look at yourself in the mirror and you're not happy going in there. I think that's a terrible trap that we should all try to avoid as we navigate our career paths and find the thing that's most optimal for us. Which is usually a mix of career success, but also meaningfulness and alignment in the work that we're doing with our values.
turns.zh: 有一天醒来，发现自己已到职业生涯后期，却感到被困住了——因为你已经习惯了某种生活方式，或者身边的人对你有某种期待，让你不得不继续做这份工作，但当你照镜子时，却并不开心。我觉得这是一个可怕的陷阱，我们在规划职业道路、寻找最适合自己的方向时，都应该尽力避免。而最适合自己的方向，通常是事业成功与工作意义感、以及与自身价值观一致性的结合。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Thanks. I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢，我很高兴来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I've heard such great things about you from a lot of people, including a bunch of guests that have been on the podcast. And you also have this really great event diagram of maybe an ideal guest for the podcast. You've done growth. You've done products. You've started a company. You're also an executive coach to founders. So there's a variety of topics I'm excited to begin too. So thanks again for being here.
turns.zh: 我从很多人那里听到过你的好评，包括一些上过这档播客的嘉宾。而且你自己也画了一张很棒的活动图，简直就是这档播客理想嘉宾的画像。你做过增长，做过产品，创过业，还是创始人的高管教练。所以有很多话题我都迫不及待想聊。再次感谢你的到来。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 嗯，我很兴奋能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: An interesting thing that I'll start with is that when we were chatting about what to focus on in our conversation, where you're emailing about this, and you did something that I thought was really interesting. You ran something called a Curiosity Loop where you pinged a bunch of your friends and asked them for input in this really structured way. So I thought I'd start there. Could you just share what this process is, so that we can learn how to maybe do it ourselves, this idea of a curiosity loop?
turns.zh: 我想从一个有趣的事情开始。我们在聊这期对话要聚焦什么话题的时候，通过邮件来回讨论，你做了一件我觉得特别有意思的事。你运行了一个叫「好奇心循环」的东西，给你的一堆朋友发了消息，用一种非常有结构的方式征求他们的意见。所以我想就从这里开始。你能分享一下这个流程是什么样的吗？让我们也能学会自己怎么做，这个好奇心循环的想法。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: A curiosity loop is essentially going to a whole bunch of people. In this case, I sent out an email very quickly to about 10 or 11 people and asking them, "Hey, here are nine topics for Lenny's Podcast. What are two or three of the topics that resonate with you and why?" And I got back such an incredible amount of information for about 20 minutes of work. I don't normally do this, but I actually showed you some of the anonymized feedback from people really just talking about what resonated and what didn't. So I came out of it just so much smarter, and curiosity loops are my method of doing so.
turns.zh: 好奇心循环本质上就是去找一大堆人。在这次情况下，我快速地给大约 10 到 11 个人发了一封邮件，问他们：「嘿，这里有九个 Lenny's Podcast 的话题，其中两三个最让你有共鸣的是哪些？为什么？」然后我得到了非常惊人的信息量，而我大概只花了 20 分钟。我通常不会这么做，但我当时还把一些匿名化的反馈给你看了，就是大家真实地谈哪些话题有共鸣、哪些没有。所以做完之后我变聪明了很多，而好奇心循环就是我用的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Often, people ask friends for advice on just like, "Hey, what should I do here? What can I maybe talk about on this podcast?" Your approach had a lot of structure to it. So maybe two questions just like, what is the actual structure to this concept? And then two, just people... You can often ask friends for advice, but you also don't want to over bug them with questions. How do you think about just not over asking everyone questions all the time, but all decisions you want to make? So I guess the question is, when do you use this versus just not?
turns.zh: 通常大家问朋友建议就是「嘿，我该怎么办？这个播客上聊点什么好？」但你的方法很有结构。所以可能有两个问题：一是这个概念到底有什么结构？二是大家经常可以问朋友建议，但也不想过度打扰他们。你是怎么看待不要一直问所有人问题，但又想为各种决策征求建议这件事的？所以问题是，你什么时候用这个方法，什么时候不用？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I think that there are heavyweight and lightweight ways to use this. So the heavyweight way was what I just exemplified by saying, I sent an email and I made a doc. And on the other side, I had all of this really interesting and rich data. The lightweight way to do this is really just make it your ongoing theme of what you're curious about as you interact with people. So maybe it's this thing where every single day as you talk to people, if you have a social topic, you might just bring up the same question over and over again and start looking for are there any differences or surprises in what people are telling you? One of the big reasons why I think curiosity loops are really useful is that it really fights the fact that there's a lot of bad advice out there. (00:05:54): And it's not bad because it's not well-intentioned, but it's bad because it's not contextual. So when someone tells you to quit your job and chase your dreams, or they tell you to sit tight and grind through and build some experience before you go off and go start the company that you've always been thinking about starting, which piece of advice do you actually take? Right? A lot of it depends on your situation, what you're considering, what skills and experience you actually have, and curiosity loops actually are this way of really thinking about how do you make your advice contextual. So I'll break it down a bit in terms of how I think about structuring it. So the first piece of a curiosity loop is really just thinking about asking a good question. In the time when I was working at SurveyMonkey in the past, I had this opportunity to spend a lot of time with the survey researchers, and we really talked a lot about what makes a question good. (00:06:44): So in this case, a question's good if it's specific, if it solicits rationale, and it's not biased. You don't want to start a question with, here's what I think because people have this tendency to want to please you or to agree with you. So a good example... Well, let me start with a bad example of a question. A bad example of a question is, what should I do with my career next? It's just such a poorly formed question because it's really vague, it's not specific. It puts a lot of cognitive load on other people, and the output that you're going to get from it is probably going to be similarly bad. Garbage in, garbage out. A better example of a question might be something like, "Hey, you know me. I'm a marketer. I've been thinking about doing this webdev thing. So my plan is to quit my job, do a webdev bootcamp and then go find a job elsewhere. Do you think that's a good idea?" (00:07:45): There's just so much rich data to actually explore with that. First, are you suited to being a developer? Are webdev boot camps effective? What's the state of the economy in the hiring market right now for junior web developers? And that's an example of maybe a question that's a little bit more specific and gives people something to anchor on. So that's the first piece. The next piece is really around how do you curate who you ask? I think there are two dimensions of this. The first one is the obvious one, which is a subject matter expert who really knows something about the topic at hand. So maybe a webdev themselves, for my example question. Another one, and this dimension I think is really important, is someone who knows you really well and can provide insight on how well does that work for you. And then after that, you really want to ask the question. And this touches on what you said about how do you make it really lightweight? (00:08:41): Ask the question in a way that really gets you a useful constructive answer, but doesn't put too much weight on people. So what I usually like to do is just make it very lightweight. So in your case, I said, "Here are nine topics. Can you pick your top two and tell me why you like them?" Some people went above and beyond and scrolled through and gave me feedback on every single topic. Some of them just said, "Here are my top two, and here's one I think you should avoid." I wanted to design it in a way where if you're a busy founder, you're a busy product person, which is the list that I chose for this curiosity loop, you would be able to sit down on your couch at the end of the night, read this interesting email and tap out a quick reply and give me that answer. Because the risk that you're running is either you're getting poor answers or you're getting a really low response rate because you've given them way too much cognitive load in terms of answering it. (00:09:35): And then finally, to close the loop, I think a big piece of it is processing that information and then thanking them for it. So a big misconception that people have when they're really getting into this work of asking for advice or input from other people in the community is often that it's really one-sided. I'm asking you for help and you're getting nothing out of it. The reminder that I would have for all of you is that it feels really good to help someone. It feels really good to be heard and give input. And a big piece of that is, if someone comes to you and they said, "You gave me this advice, it changed my life. Maybe it's not at that level, but it really affected my decision and here's how it turned out. Thank you so much." That feels so good, especially if you only spent a few minutes giving them the input that enabled them to make a better decision.
turns.zh: 我觉得有重量级和轻量级两种用法。重量级的用法就是我刚才举的例子：发一封邮件，建一个文档，然后你就得到了这些非常有趣、丰富的数据。轻量级的做法则是把它作为你与人互动时持续的好奇主题。也许是这样的：每天你和别人聊天时，如果你有一个社交话题，你可以反复提起同一个问题，然后观察大家给你的回答里有没有差异或意外之处。我觉得好奇心循环非常有用的一个重要原因是，它真的能对抗一个事实——这个世界上有太多糟糕的建议。(00:05:54)：这些建议糟糕不是因为出发点不好，而是因为不结合语境。当有人劝你辞职追梦，或者劝你沉下心来积累经验再出去创业，你到底该听谁的？对吧？这很大程度上取决于你的处境、你在考虑什么、你实际拥有什么技能和经验。好奇心循环就是一种让你的建议变得有语境的方法。我来拆解一下我是怎么思考它的结构的。好奇心循环的第一步就是想清楚怎么问一个好问题。我之前在 SurveyMonkey 工作时，有机会和很多调研研究员一起共事，我们经常讨论什么才是一个好问题。(00:06:44)：在这种情况下，一个问题如果是具体的、能引出理由的、不带偏见的，那就是好问题。不要用「我是这么想的」来开头，因为人有讨好你、附和你的倾向……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to summarize, I wrote these pieces down. The concept broadly is if you want advice on a decision you're trying to make, pick some friends and this is... I guess I'll go through the four things you just mentioned. And part two is actually pick the right friends. But one is just, come up with a question that's specific. As in just like, what should I do with my life? But more, should I take the specific role at the specific company? Figure out the people that know you well and maybe have some context on this decision. How many people do you usually email for this sort of thing? What's a number?
turns.zh: 所以总结一下，我把这几点记下来了。整体概念是，如果你想就某个决策征求建议，就选一些朋友——我想把你刚提到的四点过一遍。第二部分是选对朋友。但第一点就是，想一个具体的问题。不是「我这辈子该怎么办」这种，而是「我该不该接这家公司这个具体职位」这种。找出那些了解你、对这个决策有一定背景的人。你通常会给多少人发邮件？大概多少个？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I would try to optimize for getting at least three or four responses. It just depends on the nature of the loop. And then you think about what is your response rate. So if you're emailing really busy people that you don't know very well, maybe you would assume that you only get half of people to respond. If you're emailing people really well and it's really lightweight like, yes or no, and here's why, then you might just send out a handful.
turns.zh: 我会尽量优化到至少收到三四个回复。这取决于这个循环的性质。然后你要想你的回复率是多少。如果你发的是很忙、不太熟的人，那可能只有一半人会回复。如果你发的是很熟的人，而且问题很轻量，比如是或不是，再加上为什么，那你可能就发几个就够了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. So it's five to 10 people, broadly sounds like. Oh yeah, you want to make it really quick and easy. So it's like, here's 10 things, which of these two do you think I should focus on? So it's a quick ask as something you recommend, and then just thank them for it after you finish. Is that broadly the approach?
turns.zh: 好的，太好了。所以大概是 5 到 10 个人，听起来是这样。哦对，你要让它非常快速简单。就是「这里有 10 个选项，你觉得我该专注哪两个？」这是一个快速的请求，你建议这样做，然后完成后感谢他们。这大概就是整体方法？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yep, that's the approach. One thing I want to note is that it's actually really useful for personal things as well. So we framed it in this professional context of, I'm trying to change a job. But one example that I have is when we had our daughter who's now three years old, one of the debates that my partner and I were having was how do we actually set up our estate planning in terms of if, God forbids, something happened to both of us. How should she inherit the state? And my partner was basically saying, "18 years old, she gets everything fully unlocked." I was saying, "Oh, well maybe 25." And we're at this impasse. And we actually just started to tell each other, why don't we, in our day-to-day conversations with folks that we trust in our family, people that we think are smart, that have kids ask people what their perspective is on it. (00:12:28): One thing was really telling, no one out of everyone we asked said 18. So that really dragged my partner up. And then the other thing that was really interesting was that we learned a little bit about executive function and the research around it. So executive function, which is your ability to make decisions and plans and be thoughtful peaks at the age of 30, and it's all downhill from there. So bad news for people like me that are older.
turns.zh: 对，就是这个方法。有一点我想提的是，它在个人事务上也非常有用。我们之前把它框定在了职业语境下，比如「我想换工作」。但我有一个例子：当我们有了女儿，她现在三岁了，我伴侣和我之间的一个争论是——如果我们俩万一出了什么事，该怎么安排遗产继承？我伴侣的基本立场是「18 岁，全部解锁」。我说「嗯，也许 25 岁」。我们僵持不下。于是我们就在日常和信任的家人、聪明的、有孩子的朋友聊天时，顺便问他们的看法。(00:12:28)：有一件事很说明问题——我们问的所有人里，没有一个人说 18 岁。这让我伴侣的预期上调了。另一件很有意思的事是，我们了解了一些关于执行功能（executive function）的研究。执行功能就是你做决策、做计划、深思熟虑的能力，它在 30 岁达到顶峰，之后就走下坡路了。所以对我这种年纪大一点的人来说是个坏消息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then I'm getting [inaudible 00:12:54] or game over.
turns.zh: 然后我就[听不清 00:12:54] 或者说游戏结束了。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just like I'm-
turns.zh: 就像我——

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: But if you're thinking about 18, you are so far from your peak. So it dragged us both up in terms of what our set point was to make a decision like that. But we wouldn't have figured that out without a curiosity loop because it's too much work to dig through papers or research or whatever else to try to come to a good decision on it.
turns.zh: 但如果你考虑的是 18 岁，那离顶峰还差得远呢。所以这件事把我们俩的基准点都往上拉了。但如果没有好奇心循环，我们是想不到这一点的，因为要去翻论文、翻研究、想据此做出好决策，工作量太大了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the core lesson here is just, versus just emailing a bunch of people, asking for advice, which I imagine people often do, just what should I do here? Creating a little bit of the structure and even calling it a curiosity loop, I bet, helps people feel like they want to be a part of this and participate and help.
turns.zh: 所以这里的核心教训就是，相比于只是群发邮件问建议——我想很多人都会这么做，就是「我该怎么办」——加一点结构，甚至给它起个名字叫「好奇心循环」，我猜会让大家更想参与、更想帮忙。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. One of the things that I always try to do is I try to explain to people in my ask, here's why I picked you. So for example, I picked you because I really trust you to be a sound source of truthful advice and give me some feedback. So I really value that. Do you mind spending a couple of minutes and just giving me some thoughts on this?
turns.zh: 对，definitely。我一直努力做的一件事是在请求里解释「我为什么找你」。比如，我找你是因为我真的信任你能给出真实可靠的建议和反馈，我非常看重这一点。你能不能花几分钟，给我一些想法？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how often are you pinging people? If you're a friend of Ada, are you getting curiosity looped every week, or how often? What's your rate limit?
turns.zh: 那你大概多久会打扰大家一次？如果你是 Ada 的朋友，是每周都会被好奇心循环一次，还是多久一次？你的频率限制是什么？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I usually reserve it for bigger things. So probably quarterly or anything where I'm having a big debate, and I'm feeling really indecisive.
turns.zh: 我通常把它留给比较大的事情。大概每季度一次，或者任何我正在经历大纠结、特别犹豫不决的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. It also makes me think about this idea of a personal board of directors, and this feels like an asynchronous approach to that concept where instead of a call every, I don't know, quarter month with small group, it's asynchronous. Here's an ask I have-
turns.zh: 太棒了。这也让我想到「个人董事会」这个概念，感觉这就是它的异步版本——不是每月或每季度和一小群人开个电话会，而是异步的。「这是我的一个请求——」

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Totally. Yep. I think this is really based off of the marketing concept of customer advisory councils. So when I was working in marketing and product at a startup, one of the things we would always have is a group of our top customers on DM, basically. And if we had really interesting product conflicts, we would actually just go ping a couple of them and ask them, "Hey, we're debating this. Do you mind just giving us your quick thoughts and telling us why?" And then being able to as a marketer come back to the product conversation and say, here is the literal voice of the customer and four or five different verbatims on what people think about this really enabled me as a marketer to have a seat at the table. And the insight and the helpfulness of that was really something I wanted to bring to my personal life as well.
turns.zh: 完全同意。对。我觉得这其实源自营销里「客户顾问委员会」的概念。我之前在创业公司做营销和产品时，我们总会有一批顶级客户在 DM 里。如果我们有很纠结的产品问题，就会去 ping 其中几个，问「嘿，我们在纠结这个，你介意快速说说你的想法和理由吗？」然后作为营销负责人回到产品讨论里说「这就是客户原话，四五条原汁原味的反馈」，这让我在产品决策桌上有了话语权。这种洞察和价值，我也想带到个人生活中来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting. It's basically user research for your life. User research, you're told don't do what people tell you to do. I guess it's the same thing here, where it's just like, here's advice and then you end up making the decision for your own own life.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。基本上就是你生活版的用户研究。做用户研究时，别人告诉你不要照着用户说的做。这里也一样，建议只是输入，最终决策还是你自己做。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Right. Right. Yes. That is the big caveat. Don't do what people tell you to do. Take it as an input and look for the hard feedback. Look for things that you strongly disagree with or are surprises to you. Because to me, I think these loops are more about looking around the corner and seeing if there's anything you missed in terms of the integrity of your decision making process.
turns.zh: 对，对，是的。这就是最大的 caveat——不要照别人说的做。把它当作输入，去找那些难听的反馈，找那些你强烈不同意或让你意外的点。因为对我来说，这些循环更多是帮你看到拐角后面、看你的决策过程有没有遗漏什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. You said that people told you what we should not talk about. They're like, "Don't cover this." What was in that list?
turns.zh: 好的。你说大家告诉了你我们不该聊什么。他们说「别聊这个」。那个清单里有什么？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: So I think there were two topics on the list. The first one, it was just how do you onboard and hire and bring people onto the team? And the feedback I got there was like, "There's just so many people who have done this. I'm sure you have some interesting concepts, but I personally wouldn't be that interested in hearing it. And that was really useful to me. And then the other one was actually just about being a woman in Silicon Valley and the experience of that. I actually had someone write, and you probably read this, Lenny, "No. Stay far away from this. There's no winning on this topic."
turns.zh: 清单上有两个话题。第一个是如何 onboarding、招聘、把人带入团队。我收到的反馈是「做这件事的人太多了。我确定你有些有意思的观点，但我个人不会太想听」。这对我很有用。另一个话题是关于在硅谷做女性的体验。实际上有人直接写——你可能也读到了，Lenny——「别碰。离这个话题远点。这个话题没赢面。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, my God. Okay, let's touch on that topic rather than, it's going to be great.
turns.zh: 天哪。好的，那我们偏要碰一碰这个话题，会很精彩的。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah. So let's ignore the advice?
turns.zh: 好。所以我们就忽略这个建议？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's ignore it. Before we get to that, I wanted to first talk about you. You gave me some homework also ahead of this chat. And the homework was around helping me figure out values and personal values for myself. I did the exercise. So first of all, can you just maybe talk about what this exercise was, and what the goal of it is? And then I'll share what I come up with.
turns.zh: 对，忽略它。在聊那个之前，我想先聊聊你。你在这次聊天前也给我留了作业。作业是帮我梳理我的个人价值观。我做了这个练习。所以首先，你能聊聊这个练习是什么、目标是什么吗？然后我分享我得出的结果。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: So the homework that I gave you is similar homework that I give to everyone that I work with in coaching, and it's this values exercise. It's this 10 to 15 minute exercise where you're presented with a list of words that might encompass potential values. It's pretty lightweight. You just go down the list, and you pick out all the words that resonate with you, and then we filter them down into groups of values, and then we filter them down into a stack rank and a list. And the output on the end is basically three to five sentences that cover what are the values stack rank that are important to you right now in your personal and professional life? And what I really like is, it's this internal scorecard of what really matters to you in your decision making process as opposed to the external scorecard of status, money, wealth, how other people perceive you, that often we feel really pressured by. So it's this great way to look back and see how well do decisions, or how well do my situations in life align with my values?
turns.zh: 我给你留的作业，和我在教练中给每个人留的作业一样，就是价值观练习。这是一个 10 到 15 分钟的练习，你会看到一份可能涵盖各种价值观的词语列表。它很轻量。你顺着列表往下走，挑出所有让你有共鸣的词，然后我们把它分组，再排个优先级。最终输出大概是三到五句话，覆盖你目前个人和职业生活中最重要的、排好序的价值观是什么。我很喜欢的一点是，它是你的「内部记分卡」——在你决策过程中真正重要的是什么，而不是「外部记分卡」——地位、金钱、财富、别人怎么看你——那种我们经常感到压力的东西。所以它是一个很好的回头看的方式：我的决策、我的处境和我的价值观契合度如何？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. And what I liked about it is, if someone were to be like, "Hey, come up with your values." I'd be like, "Oh, my God. I'm just sitting here thinking about words and concepts." And it was really helpful because it was basically multiple choice. Here's all the options across tons of categories, just keep picking and then helps you whittle them down. I ended up with six. I feel like that's one too many. Actually, I added a bonus one because it's just one that I really like. But should I read through what I came up with?
turns.zh: 好的。我喜欢它的一点是，如果有人跟我说「来，想出你的价值观」，我会想「天哪，我就坐这儿想词和概念吗」。但它很有帮助，因为基本上是选择题。这里有所有类别下的所有选项，你一直选，然后它帮你慢慢缩减。我最后得出六个。我觉得多了一个。其实我还加了一个额外的，因为我真的很喜欢它。但我应该先把我得出的念一遍吗？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, that sounds great.
turns.zh: 好，听起来很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So here's what my values, I guess. Choose adventure, stay optimistic, treat others you want to be treated. Classic. Keep getting better, act generously. And added one that my grandma taught me back in the day that has stuck with me, that had nothing to do with this exercise, but I just wanted to have on this list, which is, first do what you need to do, and then do what you want.
turns.zh: 所以这就是我的价值观。选择冒险，保持乐观，待人以你希望被对待的方式。经典。持续精进，慷慨行事。还加了一个我奶奶当年教我、一直留在我心里的，跟这个练习无关，但我就是想列上——先做你该做的，再做你想做的。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I love it. What a great list of values and what stands out to me from that list too, Lenny, is this idea of achievement or status or success. A lot of the things that we talk about publicly, what your LinkedIn feed might look like don't actually show up in your values. And it must reflect in some of the choices that you've made in your life.
turns.zh: 我喜欢它。多棒的一份价值观清单啊，Lenny。这份清单里让我印象深刻的是——成就、地位、成功这些东西，我们公开聊的、你 LinkedIn 动态里会出现的那些，其实并不在你的价值观里。这一定也体现在你人生中做的一些选择上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, I hope so.
turns.zh: 是的，希望如此。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Let me ask you this. Let's try to apply some of the values in real time as an experiment.
turns.zh: 我问你个问题。我们来做一个实验，实时应用一下这些价值观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, boy.
turns.zh: 哎呀。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: If you think about a recent decision that you've had to make or a decision that you're facing coming up, can you share what that decision might be? And then let's try to apply the values to it to think about if you were living up to these values, what choice would you make and maybe some of the pressures you might feel to choose otherwise.
turns.zh: 如果你想一个你最近必须做的决策，或即将面临的决策，你能分享一下是什么决策吗？然后我们试着把价值观套上去——如果你要践行这些价值观，你会做什么选择？以及你可能会感受到的、让你偏离它们的压力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So an ongoing decision I have is I have all these opportunities of things I can be doing. Additional things I can be doing. The podcast, this actually was a good example of I never wanted to do a podcast because I really wanted to... Life is good. I was writing this newsletters, doing great, making a living, doing one great email a week. And I was like, "Why would I do anything more? This is good." So I've constantly resisted, I resisted the podcast for two to three years, and then eventually succumbed. And it was a great decision in the end. But now, I have other things that I'm trying to not do, but they're always pushing into my mind space like, a book for example. Of course at one point, and I paused that just so I could have more time for the podcast. So I guess the decision is just like, what should I say yes to versus say no to? (00:20:26): I'm looking at my values a little bit, and one of them is choose adventure, which you would think would be just do stuff, just try stuff out. But I feel like maybe it's just a missing bullet point here of, I just want to do less. I'm trying to take on less and do less and cut out and-
turns.zh: 我一直在纠结的一个决策是，我有这一堆可以做的事情的机会。那些额外的事情。播客其实就是一个好例子——我从来不想做播客，因为我真的很想……生活挺好的，我在写 newsletter，做得不错，靠每周一封好邮件就能养活自己。我就想「我干嘛还要做别的？挺好的」。所以我一直抵制，抵制了两三年，最后还是做了。结果是个很棒的决定。但现在，我又有一堆别的事情在试着不做，但它们总是挤进我的脑海，比如写书。当然到某个时候——我之前把书搁置了，就是为了给播客腾时间。所以这个决策其实就是，我该对什么说 yes，对什么说 no？(00:20:26)：我在看我的价值观，其中一条是选择冒险，你会觉得这就是去做事、去尝试。但我感觉它可能少了一条，就是「我只想少做点事」。我一直在尝试少承担、少做事、做减法——

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: That's really interesting.
turns.zh: 这很有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... simplify. Yeah. Because there's just endless things I could be doing, and I want to spend time with my wife. And now, my new child is coming in a couple of months, if all goes well. So that's where my mind goes when you ask that.
turns.zh: ……简化。对。因为有太多太多我可以做的事，而我想陪老婆。而且再过几个月，如果一切顺利，我的孩子就要出生了。所以你问这个问题时，我脑子里想的就是这些。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And then maybe if you were to decompose adventure, what adventure actually means to you and you go into that word list, you might actually just find that some of these opportunities like writing a book, at some point, it doesn't feel like an adventure.
turns.zh: 嗯，嗯。然后如果你去拆解「冒险」到底是什么意思，回到那个词表，你可能会发现，像写书这种机会，到某个点它就不像冒险了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. That's so true. The beginning of it is an adventure. And then that's such a good point because yeah, once you start a thing... Something I always say about this content creation life is like, it's easy to start. It's hard to keep it going, and it becomes just this treadmill of just, you have to keep creating awesome stuff basically for the rest of your life. I don't know how you get off the treadmill. Not that I'm complaining, but that's just a reality of this path. So that is such a good point that it becomes not adventurous very quickly. So that's really interesting.
turns.zh: 对。太对了。它的开始是冒险。这一点太好了，因为一旦你开始一件事……关于这种内容创作的生活我常说的一句话是：开始容易，持续难。它会变成一台跑步机，你余生都得不停地创造好内容。我不知道怎么下这台跑步机。不是我在抱怨，这就是这条路的现实。所以你说的太对了——它很快就变得不再冒险了。这真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess the other thing is just, what's a cutoff? What am I... I do a bunch of angel investing and so I'm thinking about just stopping that for a while just so I get up more time with my new child and just carve out things that maybe aren't as essential.
turns.zh: 我猜另一件事就是，什么时候是个头？我在做什么……我做一堆天使投资，所以我在想是不是该停一阵子，好给即将出生的孩子腾出更多时间，也把那些可能没那么必要的事情砍掉。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: So on the values exercise, I think what you've done a really good job of is just really delineating, here are some examples of choices that you have to make. I think that there are some points in our lives where writing a book, it just seems really obvious. It's good for your career. It's the next level in terms of where you go from the community, the newsletter, the podcast and getting to that next level. But where I think there is value is these lists of values can help ground us from those obvious decisions. So in my life, to share a mini example of this, there have been a lot of cases where the next obvious step for me might be to go an executive at a big company and to go chase the dream and continue on the latter climb of my career. (00:22:40): As I've examined my own personal values, a big piece of it has really been around prioritizing relationships and really pursuing knowledge and growth on my own terms. And things like independence and autonomy have started to creep up over time, especially once I started a family. It became very clear to me that sometimes the external scorecard of what people think you should go do is very much an opposition of what I actually want to do. Even though it might be objectively better, depending on what scorecard you actually use, I would actually be less happy with some of those outcomes. So I think values are this really nice useful tool to think about how do you make better decisions again to maximize for your own alignment with life.
turns.zh: 在价值观练习上，我觉得你做得很好的一点是，你很清楚地列出了「这些是我需要做的一些选择」。我觉得我们人生中有些时刻，写书看起来非常理所当然——它对你的事业有好处，从社群、newsletter、播客再往上走一个台阶就是这样。但我认为价值在于，这份价值观清单能帮我们从那些「理所当然」的决策里抽身。分享一个我自己的小例子：有很多情况，对我来说下一个理所当然的步骤可能是去大公司做高管，去追梦，继续往上爬。(00:22:40)：但当我审视自己的价值观时，很大一部分是关于把关系放在首位，以及按自己的节奏追求知识和成长。像独立和自主这些，随着时间推移越来越重要，尤其是成家之后。我很清楚地意识到，有时候别人觉得你该去做的事这种「外部记分卡」，和我真正想做的事是相反的。即使从某些记分卡来看它客观上更好，但那些结果里有些会让我更不开心。所以价值观是一个很好的工具，帮你思考如何做出更好的决策，让你与生活的契合度最大化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an important point. It connects back to the course that I taught and then this potential book of, it just feels like an obvious thing I should do. It was great, but it just didn't bring me joy. And other things bring me more joy. So it was a really good reminder of just like, do I really want to be doing this, or is this just a thing that feels like a smart thing to do but maybe isn't for me psychologically? So I love just the reminder of coming back to values as a lens to decide if you want to do a thing versus just, what are people telling you? Smart or... Which just feels like the natural thing to do.
turns.zh: 这一点太重要了。它和我教的那门课、以及可能的那本书联系起来——就是感觉是理所当然该做的事。它很棒，但它没给我带来快乐。别的事给我更多快乐。所以这是一个很好的提醒：我是真的想做这件事，还是这只是看起来聪明、但心理上并不适合我？所以我很喜欢这个提醒——把价值观当作一个镜头来决定要不要做一件事，而不是听别人说「聪明」或者觉得「这就是顺理成章的下一步」。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, and it's really self-aware of you too. I think too. Cut it off because you start realizing that you're doing this course, and it's not giving you energy or it's not quite the right thing. It's really hard to say no to things.
turns.zh: 对，你这点非常 self-aware。我是这么觉得的。砍掉它，因为你开始意识到你在做这门课，它没给你能量，或者不太对。说「不」真的很难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It is. It is.
turns.zh: 确实。确实。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: And I don't think we focus on that enough.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们对这一点强调得不够。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've learned how to do that better. I have all these auto templates of ways to say no in different ways. Actually, ChatGPT, somebody's tweeted this that it has all kinds of good suggestions. If you could ask it, how do I say no to my manager who wants me to prioritize a feature? And has all kinds of clever words to [inaudible 00:24:30].
turns.zh: 嗯，我学会了更好地拒绝。我有一堆自动模板，用各种方式说 no。其实 ChatGPT——有人发推说过——它有各种好建议。你问它「我该怎么拒绝一个想让我优先做某个功能的经理？」它就有一堆巧妙的话术[听不清 00:24:30]。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Oh. Yeah, that's a great use for it.
turns.zh: 哦。对，这倒是个好用途。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing that I realized as we were going through this exercise that I imagine you find also is when you come up with an initial set of values, I was realizing I maybe another value of just keeping things simple, simplifying. And I imagine that's part of the process of narrowing in on what's important to you is you take this first pass and then you try to use it in making a decision and then you realize, oh, there's this other thing that's really important to me and that updates your values.
turns.zh: 在做这个练习时我意识到的另一件事是——我想你也发现了——当你得出初版价值观时，我意识到可能还有一个价值观就是保持简单、简化。我猜这也是这个过程的一部分：在重要的事情上聚焦，你先做第一版，然后在决策中试用，然后发现「哦，还有这个对我也很重要」，于是更新你的价值观。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, I think you could definitely use that process to force yourself to make a stack ring and to be really clear, and also change it. Change it. It's yours. So change it over time as it suits you.
turns.zh: 对，你完全可以把这个过程用来逼自己做个排序、想清楚，而且也去改它。改它。它是你的。所以随着时间、随你的需要去改它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. It feels like there should be a curiosity loop AI bot with your values that you email, what should I do with this decision? And then it's like, oh, you think simplicity is great? You should not do this.
turns.zh: 好的。感觉应该有个好奇心循环 AI 机器人，带着你的价值观，你发邮件问「这个决策我该怎么办？」然后它说「哦，你觉得简单很重要？那别做这个。」

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: The next big idea.
turns.zh: 下一个大点子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go. Somebody build that. Okay, so it's funny we went into reverse interview, and then I have to asking questions again. So let's do this. You talked about your career and how you resisted these shiny object opportunities to focus on the thing that you were excited about and wanted to do. So maybe a couple questions there. One is just early career advice. You coach a lot of founders. You had a really in incredible career doing all kinds of interesting things. What have you learned about what works best for optimizing in your early career?
turns.zh: 有了。谁来做一个。好的，真有趣，我们反客为主了，变成我在问问题了。我们换个方式。你聊到你的职业，聊到你如何抵制那些花里胡哨的机会，专注于你兴奋的、想做的事。所以这块可能有两个问题。一是关于早期职业建议。你教练很多创始人。你自己也有过非常精彩的职业，做过各种有趣的事。关于早期职业如何优化，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: My early career was pretty wild. So I had a really fast run. Over the course of seven years, I went from my first job, which was basically this entry level sales job at Microsoft, working on Microsoft adCenter to SVP of marketing at SurveyMonkey, leading a global team. And when I reflect back on what works across my early career, it really comes down in a nutshell to this career concept of explore and exploit, which actually sounds dark now that I'm saying it out loud, but-
turns.zh: 我的早期职业挺疯狂的。我跑得很快。七年时间里，我从第一份工作——微软 adCenter 的一个入门级销售——做到了 SurveyMonkey 的营销高级副总裁，带一个全球团队。我回顾早期职业什么有效时，归结起来就是这个职业概念：探索与利用（explore and exploit）。说出来现在听起来有点黑暗，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, sounds great. I love it.
turns.zh: 哈哈，听起来很棒。我喜欢。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Explore and exploit, if you're familiar with it from growth background, is really just around what mode you're in. You're either in a mode of explorer where you have a bunch of unknowns and you're testing to see whether or not you like it, how well it works, whether or not it fits for you. Or you're exploiting, where you actually have found something that's really rich and really deep and then you're just trying to get more. And when I think about explore and exploit for early career, it's all about exploration. You really haven't experienced that much, but you're doing it with a thesis. You're doing it with that growth mindset where you have a hypothesis. So coming out of school, my first job was at Microsoft. I was at adCenter. The big thing I learned from the 367 days that I was there was that corporate life at that point in my career was just a little bit too slow-paced for me, and I was really hungry to go do something else. (00:27:19): But I also learned quite a lot about marketing and advertising. And I had the suspicion that not only did I want to try something smaller, but I also wanted to try marketing. So I moved to this series a startup where I had to sample my desk on the first day called Mochi Media. And I was in a marketing role at a startup and had this great run there over three years, where I learned all kinds of things and even tried product at some point. What I learned from that experience was then I love marketing, games was pretty fun and being in a smaller team was really dynamic. It was this choice on, do I exploit and go deeper into the industry or do I explore more? I was 23 at the time, so I decided I have so little to lose, let me continue exploring. My big thesis was, let me try being a founder. So then I founded Connected, and Connected was this personal CRM that's a little bit like Clay. (00:28:14): If you've seen Clay now recently, in terms of how do you do a better job of managing and building your professional and personal network and-
turns.zh: 探索与利用，如果你有增长背景应该很熟，它说的是你处于什么模式。你要么在探索模式——有一堆未知，你在测试自己喜不喜欢、效果如何、适不适合你；要么在利用模式——你已经找到又富又深的东西，然后就是想从中获得更多。当我把探索与利用套到早期职业上时，它全是关于探索。你经历得还很少，但你带着一个 thesis 去探索，带着成长型思维，带着假设去探索。所以刚毕业时，我的第一份工作在微软，在 adCenter。我在那 367 天里学到的一大件事是，那个时候的公司生活对我来说节奏太慢了，我非常渴望去做点别的。(00:27:19)：但我也学到了很多关于营销和广告的东西。我隐隐觉得我不仅想试试更小的公司，还想试试营销。于是我去了 Mochi Media 这家 A 轮创业公司，第一天就得自己拼桌子。我在创业公司做营销，在那儿待了三年，学到了各种东西，甚至一度尝试了产品。我从那段经历里学到的是——我喜欢营销，游戏挺有意思，小团队很 dynamic。于是面临一个选择：是利用、深耕这个行业，还是继续探索？我当时 23 岁，所以我决定我没什么可失去的，继续探索。我的大 thesis 是：试试做创始人。于是我创办了 Connected，它是一个个人 CRM，有点像现在的 Clay。(00:28:14)：如果你最近见过 Clay 的话，就是那种帮你更好地管理和构建专业及个人……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's a beautiful product.
turns.zh: 对。是个很漂亮的产品。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, it's a beautiful product, much more beautiful than what we built at the time. It was such a great learning experience to discover what it was like to be a founder of a company and an entrepreneur. My personal learning out of all of those things was really just that I was continuously optimizing that I loved marketing. I loved being a founder. I really like small teams. There are pros and cons to this corporate life, where maybe things are really slow paced, but the scale is really important. So that was really what carried me through a lot of my early career. After Connected was acquired by LinkedIn, I moved into this exploit mode. (00:28:59): So I was at LinkedIn for a period of time while I was investing, and I really wanted to be intentional about the time that I spent there in terms of how I wanted to exploit it. So unlike a traditional path where you're really focused on trying to get the biggest title, a big team, set yourself up to run a big org, my role at LinkedIn was really explicit. I even told my manager this when I first came in, "I'm here to learn to be a better founder." So there were a lot of things when I started connected, which I didn't know how to do very well, I didn't understand growth. I was fair to middling at pricing. I really didn't understand how to build a subscriptions business and how to price it. So if I can make my LinkedIn experiences match to that, that would be a huge win for me independent of promotion, or compensation or a whole bunch of those things because the plan afterward is actually to go off and start another company. (00:29:53): So I managed to get into this great role leading gross marketing for LinkedIn, working with their growth team from a hundred million to 200 million members, read every experiment brief that I could, spent a lot of time with the team, really understanding their process, and then shifted into the subscription side where I worked on LinkedIn subscriptions and ran their sales subscriptions business at scale through the online channel. And saw how all of those pieces and worked together from a financial planning and analysis stage to all of the optimizations that they did. It was just such a rare opportunity, but I wouldn't have gotten those opportunities if I just let them promote me or I followed a strategy where I was just focused on trying to get the biggest title. (00:30:35): Instead, I was focused on those learnings and those experiences. Ultimately, the fact that I was a startup founder. I had big company experience. I had growth experience, and I had subs experience. And I was a product marketer. That was actually the winning combination that caused SurveyMonkey to send me a LinkedIn InMail, start a conversation and ultimately bring me in as their head of marketing at the age of, I think I was 27 or 28 at the time. Because their rationale was, you have all these experiences that we really need and you don't have the management experience, but we have plenty of that. We're happy to teach that to you.
turns.zh: 对，是个很漂亮的产品，比我们当时做的漂亮多了。作为公司创始人和创业者，这是一次非常棒的学习经历。我从所有这些事里学到的是，我在持续优化、我爱营销、我爱做创始人、我喜欢小团队。公司生活有它的利弊——也许节奏很慢，但规模很重要。这就是支撑我早期职业一路走来的东西。Connected 被 LinkedIn 收购后，我进入了利用模式。(00:28:59)：我在 LinkedIn 待了一段时间，同时也在做投资。我很有意识地想要想清楚在那儿的时间该怎么利用。和传统的、专注于拿更大 title、带更大团队、准备管大部门的路径不同，我在 LinkedIn 的角色目标非常明确。我甚至入职时就跟我 manager 说：「我是来学怎么做一个更好的创始人的。」我开始做 Connected 时有很多事做得不好，不懂增长，定价能力一般，也不懂怎么构建订阅业务、怎么定价。如果我在 LinkedIn 的经历能匹配上这些，那对我来说就是巨大的收获——与晋升、薪酬、那一堆东西无关，因为之后的计划是出去再创一家公司。(00:29:53)：于是我进入了一个很棒的角色，领导 LinkedIn 的增长营销，和他们的增长团队一起把会员从 1 亿做到 2 亿，读了能读到的每一份实验 brief，和团队泡在一起，真正理解他们的流程，然后转到订阅这边，做 LinkedIn 订阅，管他们的销售订阅……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this framework. I've never heard it described this way. Explore and exploit connects a lot with what I always recommend which, early on, is to optimize for a variety of experience so that you can figure out where you actually have a good time and what you're interested in versus getting stuck on the first thing something. I don't know if you'll have an immediate answer to this, but I'm curious. Many people don't know how long to stick with something that maybe doesn't feel good but may lead to something. Like, someone may be in a job right now, or just like, "I really don't like this job, but I feel like it'll lead to something great. And I don't want to give up too quickly." So I guess the question is, what are heuristics that tell you to stick it out and stick with something that you think will lead to something great versus hold the recording and get out?
turns.zh: 我非常喜欢这个框架。我没听人这么描述过。探索与利用和我一直推荐的很契合——早期要去优化经历的多样性，这样你才能发现自己到底在哪里过得开心、对什么感兴趣，而不是卡在第一件事上。我不知道你有没有现成的答案，但我很好奇。很多人不知道该坚持多久一件可能感觉不好、但可能通向更好事情的事。比如有人可能在一份工作里，「我真的不喜欢这份工作，但我觉得它会通向很好的东西，我不想放弃得太早」。所以问题是，有什么启发式信号告诉你该坚持、等它通向更好的东西，还是该及时止损、抽身而退？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: That's a great question, and it's a really tough one that is contextual on the person that you are. So one of the things that I like to share is this idea of, it's a little gory, don't be the frog. So if you are familiar with the story of the frog, it's this idea of boiling the frog. So if you take a frog, and you throw in a pot of boiling water, it'll jump out. But if you take a frog and you put in a pot and you increase the temperature degree by degree by degree, the frog doesn't notice and before it knows, it's boiled alive. And how I apply this to your question to come back and circle back to it is that, it's really easy to be a victim of inertia. It's really easy for all of us to be the frog where there are little things that make us uncomfortable, and we sit with them or we think, "Gosh, it'll get better. The next manager will get better. I'm always one conversation or one promotion away from getting to that next step." (00:33:02): But you really have to be aware of your surroundings. You have to be aware of which way is the direction of the temperature of the water trending. That's what makes the advice really contextual. I really look at it from the lens of learning. What can I learn here, and how am I growing and developing? So there might be an argument for you to stay at a job for two decades. If it turns out that every single day you're being really challenged, you're learning new things, you're deriving a lot of meaningful enjoyment out of your work and you're this happy frog that's hanging out, realizing that things are good and the temperature is not rising. But there are also situations where you might encounter just some really hard walls, where you don't get along with the thesis of the company. You don't agree with the direction of the company that you're in. (00:33:53): There are fundamental aspects of the role which are limiting to you or you're not learning a lot, frankly. I think that happens a lot, where you providing a lot of value and doing a good job at a company, but you might not be learning things that stretch you and grow you to achieve your ultimate goal. When you are aware of that learning, I think that's the point at which you have to say, "How do I change that? How do I be an agent in my own career and make a difference in that?" And it doesn't necessarily mean that the strategy is to quit your job and do something catastrophic, and then go do something else, take a course or sign up for something new. It might actually mean a proactive conversation with your manager or the leadership to say, "I love what I'm doing here, and I would also like to learn a little bit more. And here's what I'm interested in." (00:34:44): And then try to find a way to either land the right projects. So in my case, it was really growth and subscriptions, that experience that I really wanted. Let's say, you hit a blank wall there, even take it as a gift of time, which is great. I'm not going to be able to get this from my company, but now that I have this extra time because I'm so optimized at this job, how am I going to choose to use that time? And it might be around building relationships with some of the key people at the company or learning something new on your own time that you can leverage in another way.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题，也非常难，因人而异。我想分享的一个东西是——有点血腥——「别做那只青蛙」。如果你熟悉那个故事，就是温水煮青蛙。如果你把一只青蛙扔进沸水里，它会跳出来。但如果你把青蛙放进锅里，一度一度地加温，它不会察觉，等它意识到时已经被煮死了。我把这个套回你的问题上——我们很容易成为惯性的受害者。我们很容易成为那只青蛙：有些小事让我们不舒服，我们忍受，或者想「会好起来的，下个领导会更好，我离下一步永远只差一次对话或一次晋升」。(00:33:02)：但你必须对环境保持警觉。你必须警觉水温的趋势是什么方向。这就是为什么这个建议因人而异。我从学习的镜头看：我能在这里学到什么？我在怎么成长和发展？所以也许有理由在一份工作待二十年——如果每天你都被挑战、学新东西、从工作中获得很多意义感，你就是一只开心的青蛙，意识到事情挺好、水温没在上升。但也有些情况你会撞上硬墙——你不认同公司的方向、不认同公司的 thesis。(00:33:53)：有些角色层面的根本性因素限制了你，或者坦白说你学不到多少东西。我觉得这很常见——你提供很多价值……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. Make the most of the time, even if it's not the best opportunity for you. Also love the frog boiling metaphor.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。即使不是最好的机会，也要充分利用这段时间。也很爱那个煮青蛙的比喻。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Little gory.
turns.zh: 有点血腥。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, it's great. So I guess the lesson there is think about are you that frog being boiled right now and think ahead, is this going to be the end of the-
turns.zh: 不，很棒。所以我想那里的教训就是想想你是不是正在被煮的那只青蛙，然后往前看，这是不是会——

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Right. Keep an eye on your environment and which way is it trending?
turns.zh: 对。留意你的环境，它在往哪个方向走？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the temperature on the thermostat in your office. The other thing this makes me think about is, it's so easy to get caught up in making your resume look amazing and continuing to just like, "Oh, if I get this next role, my resume's going to look so great." And this other logo and this cool title and role. I find that just like, you do that long enough in your life, you end up... You retire, and then you die. Life is that resume. Right? That is your life, you're living, and there's not going to be a point at which you have to realize, okay, I've done all the things to make my resume. Also, I'm like, "What do I actually want to do? Am I enjoying this?" Because it'll never end. You're never going to end trying to make a better resume and a more awesome background for yourself. Do you experience that with yourself or other people you work with of just over optimizing to make an awesome series of roles and logos and then forgetting, do I actually enjoy any of this? What am I doing?
turns.zh: 嗯，办公室恒温器上的温度。这件事让我想到的另一点是，太容易陷进去美化简历了——「如果我拿到下一个职位，我简历会很漂亮」。又一个 logo，又一个酷 title 和职位。我发现如果你这么做足够久，你最后……退休，然后死掉。生活就是那份简历。对吧？那就是你的生活，你在活着，而且不会有一个时刻你突然意识到「好吧，我已经把简历做完了」。另外我会想，「我到底想做什么？我享受这些吗？」因为它永远不会结束。你永远在试图做一份更好的简历、更漂亮的背景。你自己或者你共事的人有没有这种过度优化、追求一串漂亮职位和 logo、却忘了「我到底享受不享受这些？我在干什么」的经历？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I have experienced that personally a lot. I think that it may be a generational thing or it just may be my background, but having grown up with the Asian tiger parenting, it's very focused on logos or certain accomplishments or certain achievements like, going to an Ivy League school, working in a company that someone's heard of, being able to have a certain title. At a certain point, I bailed out a bit and I really started to think about who am I trying to please and optimize for? That values exercise that I had you do, Lenny, is actually a big piece of that. So I probably took it for the first time over a decade ago, at this point. I looked at those values and I said, "Well, if I draw a straight line from where I am right now and just extend it forward and play the rest of the movie as it plays out, given the current plot line, how well does that optimize for those values?" (00:37:27): That's great. My parents might be happy about my resume or other people might look upon me in a certain way because I've managed these achievements, but in my day-to-day life, what really matters to me, what's really meaningful to me, only some of this stuff really matters. So getting very intentional about that and being clear about who your audience is as you navigate your career. I think it's a terrible outcome to wake up one day and be late career and feel trapped because you have a certain lifestyle or a certain expectations of the people around you that you have to go work this job, but then you look at yourself in the mirror and you're not happy going in there. I think that's a terrible trap that we should all try to avoid as we navigate our career paths and find the thing that's most optimal for us, which is usually a mix of career success, but also meaningfulness and alignment in the work that we're doing with our values.
turns.zh: 我个人深有体会。我觉得这可能是一代人的事，也可能是我背景的事。在亚洲虎妈式教育下长大，非常看重 logo、某些成就——上常春藤、在大家听过的公司工作、有某个 title。到某个点我开始有点退出，开始想：我在讨好谁、在为谁优化？我让你做的那个价值观练习，Lenny，其实就是其中很大一部分。所以我大概十多年前第一次做了它。我看着那些价值观，想：「如果我从现在画一条直线，按现在的剧情延伸下去，它对那些价值观的优化程度如何？」(00:37:27)：挺好，我父母可能为我的简历高兴，别人可能因为我有这些成就而高看我一眼。但在我的日常生活中，真正对我重要的、真正有意义的，只有其中一部分。所以非常有意识地想清楚这件事，清楚你在职业中为谁表演。我觉得有一天醒来，发现自己已到职业生涯后期却感到被困住——因为你已经习惯了某种生活方式，或者身边人对你的期待让你不得不继续这份工作，但照镜子时并不开心——这是一个可怕的陷阱，我们都该尽力避免，去找到最适合自己的东西，而那通常是事业成功与意义感、以及与价值观一致性的结合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this topic. Thank you for sharing that. This episode is brought to you by Sprig. You already heard me talk about how Sprig helps you uncover blind spots in your product development process, allowing you to better understand why users take certain actions and how they feel about the experience. Just this week, they launched their brand new templates library, which you can find at sprig.com/templates. Which helps you plug and play proven playbooks for helping you identify and solve the biggest challenges facing product teams today. From how to optimize an existing feature to improving a conversion flow, to troubleshooting drop off. One of the questions I get most on this podcast and in my newsletter is how to develop your product sense. So I decided to work with Sprig to build a playbook for how to do just that, based on my experience at Airbnb and what I learned from interviewing top product people like, Jules Walter who wrote a whole guest post on how to develop your product sense, which informed this template that you'll find. Just go to sprig.com/templates to find this playbook and 85 more that is sprig.com/templates. S-P-R-I-G.com/plates. (00:39:31): What triggered your reevaluation of that path? Was there just like a, "Oh, man. I need to really rethink where I'm going." And then I have a follow-up question.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个话题。谢谢你分享。本节目由 Sprig 赞助。你已经听我聊过 Sprig 如何帮你发现产品开发流程中的盲点，帮你理解用户为什么采取某些行为以及他们对体验的感受。就在本周，他们上线了全新的模板库，你可以在 sprig.com/templates 找到。它帮你即插即用地用上经过验证的 playbook，帮你识别和解决产品团队今天面临的最大挑战——从如何优化现有功能，到改善转化漏斗，到排查流失。这档播客和我的 newsletter 里被问得最多的问题之一就是如何培养产品感。所以我决定和 Sprig 合作，基于我在 Airbnb 的经验、以及我采访顶级产品人（比如 Jules Walter，他写过一篇关于如何培养产品感的客座文章，这个模板就借鉴了它）的所学，做一个 playbook。去 sprig.com/templates 就能找到这个 playbook 和另外 85 个。S-P-R-I-G.com/templates。(00:39:31)：是什么触发了你对那条路径的重新审视？是「天哪，我真的得重新想想我去哪」这样的时刻吗？然后我有个跟进问题。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Really just a career opportunity. And it was this step where I could do something that was, at the time, really high profile and really exciting and felt great, but also involved demanding travel and grueling hours. And wasn't in a space that I was excited about, but it looked amazing on my resume. And I was talking to a friend about it, and they actually introduced me to this values exercise to say like, "Ada, go through and fill out this values exercise, and apply it to this job." What I realized at the time, after I did it, was that my top three values, the things that I cared about this job would categorically just fail at because I would be gone all the time, in pursuit of glory that I didn't really care about. Instead, my current path at the time was something that if I persisted in, it would actually be able to potentially fulfill all of those values.
turns.zh: 其实就是一个职业机会。那一步在当时非常高调、非常 exciting、感觉很棒，但也要频繁出差、高强度工时，而且不在让我兴奋的领域，但简历上会非常好看。我和朋友聊起这事，朋友给我介绍了这个价值观练习，说「Ada，你做一下这个练习，然后套到这份工作上」。做完后我意识到，我 top 三的价值观——我最看重的——这份工作在每一条上都会彻底失败，因为我会一直不在家，去追逐我并不真正在乎的荣耀。而我当时的路径如果坚持走下去，反而有可能满足所有这些价值观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of a friend who has this metaphor of this ego monster sitting in the corner of the room that's always yelling at them, when they're... To do the thing that's impressive and take on the really cool role, and just get an awesome title, and do something really impressive, that's just like yelling at them from the corner. And my friend's just learned to just like, "Okay, that's the ego monster pulling at me. I don't have to listen to that. Doesn't mean I'm going to be happy if I listen to this guy." And that's been really helpful to my friend just to disassociate that part of the brain.
turns.zh: 这让我想到一个朋友的比喻：角落里坐着一个「自我怪兽」，一直冲他喊——去做那个很拉风的事、接那个很酷的职位、拿个 awesome 的 title、做点让人印象深刻的事，就在角落里冲他喊。我朋友学会了：「好吧，那是自我怪兽在拽我。我不一定要听它的。听了它我也不一定开心。」这对他帮助很大，就是把大脑里那一块剥离开来。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah. The ego monster is a great way to put it. I use something that Warren Buffet has talked about, which is inner scorecard versus outer scorecard.
turns.zh: 对。「自我怪兽」这个说法很好。我用的是 Warren Buffett 谈过的——内在记分卡 vs 外在记分卡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tell me more.
turns.zh: 细说说。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: So he talks about how there's an outer scorecard, which is how the rest of the world evaluates you, how you keep score in terms of external factors. So top 10 lists, wealth status, title, maybe things that people really care about. And then your inner scorecard is things that actually matter to you, how you spent your day, how good of a person you are. Did you have an adventure today, Lenny? Were you kind? And there are a lot of things that maybe are in opposition to each other. So really thinking about did you win at the cost of kindness? Did you succeed at the cost of losing access to the adventure that you really wanted? I think really thinking about it in that lens helps you trade off against some of that external pressure and the ego monster.
turns.zh: 他谈到，有一个外在记分卡——世界其他人怎么评价你、你怎么按外部因素计分。比如 top 10 榜单、财富、地位、title，那些大家很在乎的东西。然后你的内在记分卡是真正对你重要的东西——你今天怎么度过的、你是个多好的人。Lenny，你今天有没有冒险？你对人友善吗？有很多东西可能是互相冲突的。所以真的要想想：你是否以牺牲善良为代价赢了？是否以失去你真正想要的冒险为代价成功了？用这个镜头来思考，能帮你对抗那种外部压力和自我怪兽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This might be a good segue to chat about coaching. I imagine a lot of people listening to this like, "Yes, I want to do that. I want to measure myself according to my values and check in on this. And am I doing the wrong path?" It's hard to do just on your own, I find. And I think that's one of the benefits of an executive coach. So maybe we just chat about what should people know about coaching and getting a coach, and does everyone need a coach and how to think about the idea of getting a coach at some point in their career.
turns.zh: 这可能是个好过渡，聊聊教练。我想很多听众在想「是的，我想那样做，我想按我的价值观来衡量自己，检查我是不是走错了路」。但靠自己很难做到。我觉得这就是高管教练的好处之一。所以我们可以聊聊，关于教练和请教练大家该知道什么，每个人都需要教练吗，以及在职业生涯中什么时候该考虑请一个教练。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I'll have a hot take on this, and it's something that I share to people when I talk to them about coaching. But my hot take is that for the vast majority of people, they probably do not need a coach.
turns.zh: 我有个 hot take，也是我和人聊教练时常说的。我的 hot take 是，对绝大多数人来说，他们可能不需要教练。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 很好。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: And what I often push people on is if you're thinking about getting a coach, which is usually an indication that they have a feeling of being stuck or they have a problem that they're trying to solve, I ask them, "What are your goals when it comes to coaching? Roll it forward six months, what have you gotten done in your coaching experience. What have you accomplished, and you're just... It's like, a home run. And then look at all of the potential alternatives in terms of how you could have spent your valuable time and often pricey fees to achieve the same goal, but maybe in a better way." The thing that people don't really think about is if you're looking for a mentor, a coach is actually a terrible mentor in some ways because it's this one person's opinion. It's actually way better to run a curiosity loop, for example, and get the benefit a couple different minds on a specific topic and hit their wheelhouse of things that they know about. Than to go ask one person, what do you think I should do in this situation? (00:43:58): If you're trying to learn about a topic in a really robust way, let's say you want to learn about growth, maybe you should take are Reforge course and get access to all of the resources and the insights of the EIRs and the growth advisors that Reforge and get an overview and survey of the landscape instead of one person's experience and the handful of companies that they might have worked with. Likewise, if you're just feeling like you're a little emotionally overcome, I think coaches are this great resource around that, but it's actually better to pay it forward and build a tribe and a community of people around you that you can rely on for support because that's the thing that lasts you for years and years. (00:44:38): So one of the first things that I do when people talk to me about coaching is I challenge them and say, "Have you explored all of these other opportunities first, and do you really need a coach? And is a coach actually the best option for you?" Like an anti sell, just so that they know what they're getting themselves into because I don't necessarily think that it's useful for all things, even though it can be helpful.
turns.zh: 我常追问的是，如果你在考虑请教练——这通常意味着你感觉卡住了或者有个想解决的问题——我会问：「你在教练上的目标是什么？往后推六个月，你在教练经历中完成了什么？你做到了什么，才算本垒打？」然后看所有你可能用来达到同样目标、但也许更好的方式——用你宝贵的时间和往往不便宜的费用的替代方案。大家没想明白的是，如果你在找 mentor，教练其实在某种意义上是个很差的 mentor，因为这只是一个人的观点。跑一个好奇心循环、就某个话题获得几个大脑的智慧、击中他们各自的专长，其实比问一个人「我在这种情况该怎么办」要好得多。(00:43:58)：如果你想系统、扎实地学一个主题，比如你想学增长，也许你该去上 Reforge 的课，获得所有 EIR 和增长顾问的资源和洞察，获得这个领域的全景，而不是一个人的经验和那几家公司。同样，如果你只是有点情绪上扛不住，教练确实是个好资源，但更好的是 forward 付出、在你身边建一个 tribe、一个社群，因为那才是能陪伴你多年的东西。(00:44:38)：所以当有人来找我聊教练时，我第一件事就是挑战他们：「你有没有先探索过这些其他机会？你真的需要教练吗？教练是不是……」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then when do you find that it's actually important and valuable and something someone should try to get?
turns.zh: 那你什么时候觉得它真的重要、有价值、是某人该去争取的？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I wouldn't be a coach if I didn't think that it wasn't important and valuable. I think that in certain contexts it can be super helpful. So when you have situations where you're in a state of hyper growth, and you need very accelerated learning, and you need someone who can point you in the right direction, I think coaches can be really helpful. So I work with founders for example, and founders are just in this unique state where everything is chaos. They have no structure. They don't know what their jobs are. They have fully justified imposter syndrome where no one in their right mind would objectively have hired them for the position that they're in. There's really intense highs and lows. So for a founder, it might make a lot of sense to get a coach because they have to learn a lot of stuff really quickly, and time is of the essence. (00:45:54): So a coach might be a really helpful shortcut for them to get there. Related to that, I think it's also really helpful on sensitive topics. So there are a lot of things that we want to be coached on where either it takes a lot of time for us to work through and progress because it's a long-term project, for example, or it's something very sensitive. People issues and interpersonal conflicts. Coaches can be especially helpful in those cases because it's this really safe space for you to work through things, but also have someone who's really rational to help guide you through them with potentially some frameworks and extra advice.
turns.zh: 如果我觉得它不重要、没价值，我就不会做教练了。我觉得在某些情境下它非常有帮助。比如你处于高速增长中、需要非常加速的学习、需要有人给你指方向，教练可以很有帮助。比如我带的创始人，他们就处于一个独特的状态——一切混乱、没有结构、不知道自己的职责是什么、有完全合理的冒名顶替综合征（任何心智正常的人都不会客观地录用他们做他们现在的职位）、有非常剧烈的高峰和低谷。所以对创始人来说，请教练可能很有意义，因为他们必须快速学很多东西，时间就是生命。(00:45:54)：教练可能是个很好的捷径。与此相关，我觉得它在敏感话题上也很有帮助。我们想被教练的很多事，要么需要很长时间去推进因为是个长期项目，要么是非常敏感的事——人的问题、人际冲突。教练在这些情况下尤其有用，因为它是一个非常安全的空间，让你既能去消化这些东西，又有一个非常理性的人帮你、可能用一些框架和额外建议来引导你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I had a couple coaches in my career and what made me feel like I should pursue that is when you think about a sports athlete or, I don't know, athlete. No one does not have a coach, the best athletes have coaches and they get great because they have somebody helping them get better. It's not just like an accident. They don't just learn on their own. It just makes you realize that other people in their profession that have a coach helping them out are just going to be more successful because innately, they have someone helping them learn how to do the job better. So that made me realize, man, I should probably get a coach to help me out with stuff. Even though there wasn't anything super specific, I'm like, "Oh, I need to fix this problem." It was just like, wow, this just intellectually make sense. So it was actually really important and transformative for me.
turns.zh: 我职业生涯里有几个教练，让我觉得该去找一个的是——你想想运动员，呃，运动员。没有顶级运动员是没有教练的，最好的运动员都有教练，他们之所以厉害就是因为有人帮他们变得更好。这不是偶然，他们不是自己摸出来的。这会让你意识到，其他行业里有教练帮忙的人就是会更成功，因为本质上他们有人帮他们学怎么把工作做得更好。所以这让我意识到，天哪，我大概也该找个教练帮我。即使没有什么超级具体的问题说「哦，我得修这个」。就是从智识上说得通。所以它对我来说真的很重要、很 transformative。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: If you go to my site, I actually have this guide that I've written over time on both my take on how do you find a coach, and the TLDR there is actually that I strongly recommend to everyone. If you're thinking about getting a coach, talk to two or three different coaches. And really get a sense of their vibe and how well you get to know them. It's surprising because I did this piece of research, which I also wrote about, and we could link to, but I talked to over 80 people about their experiences with a coach. I talked including coaches, including founders, including executives and there's this shocking data point in there where half of people that founder their coach literally went with the first coach that they talked to. It's that your buddy said, "I work with this great coach." And then you go and you hire your buddy's coach. (00:48:08): I think that's a totally fine way to go find a coach, but I would actually really just urge people to talk to a couple because what works for your friend may not work for you. And just being able to see some of the variance in terms of the style and how people get along, I think that can make a huge difference in terms of this reflection of how do you learn best? When you think about acquiring a new skill, do you love structure? Do you not like structure? Do you like it when someone really teaches you and walks you through specific examples, or do you frameworks? Coaches come in all of those different flavors. So I think it's really worth it to explore before you get into such a deep relationship with someone, just so that both people can feel really sure about it.
turns.zh: 如果你去我的网站，我其实写了一个指南，是我随着时间写的——关于我对怎么找教练的看法。TLDR 是：我强烈建议每个人，如果你在考虑请教练，和两三个不同的教练聊聊。真正感受一下他们的 vibe、你们合不合得来。挺 surprising 的——我做过一项研究（也写过，可以链接到），我和超过 80 个人聊过他们的教练经历，包括教练、创始人、高管，里面有个惊人的数据：一半找到教练的人，literally 就是和第一个聊的教练签约了。就是你哥们说「我有个很好的教练」，然后你就去雇你哥们的教练。(00:48:08)：我觉得这完全是个可以的方式，但我真的建议大家多聊几个，因为对你朋友有效的不一定对你有效。能看看风格和合拍度的差异，我觉得会在「你怎么学得最好」这件事上产生巨大差别。当你想学一项新技能，你喜欢结构吗？不喜欢结构吗？喜欢有人手把手教、走具体例子，还是喜欢框架？教练各种风格都有。所以在进入这么深的关系之前，值得探索一下，这对双方都能更确定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's one thing that people may not think about or just something that you find really important that maybe is unexpected when you're looking for a coach?
turns.zh: 有什么大家可能想不到、但你觉得很重要、甚至有点意外的、找教练时该注意的事？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I thought that credentials and the relevant experience of the coach was a huge factor in terms of how you should go about your coach selection. But part of the interviews that I did was talking to founders that had had experiences with coaches and asking them to reflect back, and these founders and executives when they thought about it, they actually said so much more about, it was actually this amorphous sense of vibe with the person, how safe you felt with them, how deeply you would explore with them, and how well they got you, and remembered the pieces of the conversation and help you put it together. Way more than potentially some experiences that they'd had, where this person had the perfect background, but they just never really connected on that level. So it was unintuitive to me that there was such a big piece of it that was around personal connection, which is why I've now pushed people to try to talk to a couple different people. (00:49:55): And then the other thing which comes back to the sports coaching analogy is that there are different coaches that are really good at different things. So just like how, if you're a star tennis player, you might actually have multiple coaches working with you, maybe an offensive coach or a defensive coach or working on a particular swing. It actually makes sense when you're really performing at a high level to consider having coaches that work with you on shorter term basis to really just work on your speaking or help you with getting into your groove on writing or help you achieve a specific goal. You shouldn't think about it as this long-term commitment to stay with one person, but instead more choosing off of a menu and thinking about what goal are you trying to achieve right now?
turns.zh: 我原本以为教练的资质和相关经验是选教练时的大因素。但我采访的那些找过教练的创始人，当他们回想时，他们说的更多是一种很模糊的「vibe」——和这个人在一起你感觉多安全、你会探索到多深、他有多懂你、能记住对话的细节并帮你串起来——远比那些「背景完美但就是没在那个层面上连接上」的经历要多。所以让我没想到的是，个人连接居然占这么大比重，这也是为什么我现在推大家多聊几个。(00:49:55)：另一件和体育教练类比相关的是，不同的教练擅长不同的东西。就像你是个网球明星，你可能有多位教练——进攻教练、防守教练、或者专门练某个挥拍。当你在高水平表现时，考虑请教练在短期内就某个目标和你合作，其实是合理的——就练你的演讲、或帮你进入写作的状态、或帮你达成某个具体目标。你不该把它想成对一个人的长期承诺，而是更像从菜单上选，想「我现在想达成什么目标？」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Does anyone ever get multiple executive coaches that... I like how we went from, you don't need a coach to maybe need a month [inaudible 00:50:46] hamstrings.
turns.zh: 真的有人同时有多个高管教练吗……我喜欢我们从「你不需要教练」聊到了可能要雇一打[听不清 00:50:46]。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yes. I know of multiple people that I've talked to, usually CEOs, that either have had a series of coaches or have multiple coaches. It makes a lot more sense, Lenny, when you think about someone who's getting a pitch coach because they're about to get into fundraising.
turns.zh: 是的。我聊过的多个人，通常是 CEO，要么先后有过一系列教练，要么同时有多个教练。Lenny，当你想成有人请演讲教练因为要融资，这就合理多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Right. Niche skills.
turns.zh: 懂了。对。细分技能。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Right. For niche things because they're about to enter a process or someone who's trying to get into a writing coach-
turns.zh: 对。为了细分的事，因为他们要进入一个流程，或者有人想找个写作教练——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 懂了。对。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: ... in addition to some of their executive and leadership work that they might be doing.
turns.zh: ……在他们可能在做的高管和领导力工作之外。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That makes sense. I love it. I'm going to get four coaches. One for everything I do
turns.zh: 好的。有道理。我喜欢。我要请四个教练。我做什么就一个教练管一件事。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: A podcast coach.
turns.zh: 一个播客教练。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Podcast coach.
turns.zh: 播客教练。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: A newsletter coach.
turns.zh: 一个 newsletter 教练。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A writing coach, and a-
turns.zh: 一个写作教练，还有一个——

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yes. And then a parent coach. Don't forget that.
turns.zh: 对。还有一个育儿教练。别忘了这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Parent coach. A job board coach, and then just a life coach. Okay. I'm on it. Okay. So let's touch on the thing that your friends said we shouldn't touch on, which is being a woman in leadership in Silicon Valley. I guess I'll just frame it simply. Imagine there's many young women listening to this podcast, and many may dream of a career like yours, all the things you've shared. What advice do you have for young women just starting out in their career hoping to find a similar path?
turns.zh: 育儿教练。一个招聘板教练，再来个 life coach。好的，我安排上了。好，我们来聊聊你朋友说我们不该碰的那个话题——在硅谷做女性 leader。我就简单地这么问：想象有很多年轻女性在听这档播客，很多人梦想拥有像你这样的职业。你对刚起步、希望走出类似路径的年轻女性有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: This is a really delicate subject, and it's interesting because when I try to decompose why people gave me the feedback they gave me on this topic, I think a big piece of it is just that you want to have respect for the inherent challenges of being a non stereotypically great fit for leadership roles or certain career success roles in Silicon Valley and acknowledge that. And also try to push for some of the agency of the things that you can do. So I'm going to start with just this quick story about someone that I worked with who's given me permission to share this, in a coaching context and then back out. So I was working with a seed stage founder, and she's so smart. She is really dynamic, very, very focused, really, really great at taking feedback and actioning it. She's one of those people that is just stellar, and I have no doubt that she's going to make a huge dent in the universe. (00:52:58): We've been working together on Zoom for a couple of months, and I'd built this great respect for her competence as an operator, and the way that she thought and took apart problems and then acted on them. And then we met together for the first time in person at lunch. I feel almost nervous talking about this here. The disparity between my sense of who she was as an operator and how she came across to me initially at this lunch was really striking in that it was a weekday lunch and she was dressed as if she was hanging out on the weekend. So old T-shirt, hair back and in a claw, bra straps were showing. She was just incredibly casual in terms of her physical appearance. It took me almost like a little bit of a step back to reevaluate and think, "Oh, this is the same person, but she actually just presents so differently. (00:53:54): So then I took the step after we met and I gave her that feedback in one of our next coaching sessions where we invited each other to give each other feedback. I shared a lot of my impressions with her and I told her, "I respect you so much as an operator. I want to tell you that in the physical meeting that we had together, there was this disparity on how I would've potentially perceived you when I first met you in person versus what I've come to know about you from the months that we spent together." (00:54:27): Her reaction was like, "Oh my God, Ada. No one has ever connected the dots for me. Thank you so much. It has never explicitly been told to me that some of these elements which you describe, and they're very easy for me to fix and I'm motivated to fix them, are things that might actually trigger certain impressions or biases. No one's actually said it to me before, and I'm about to go into fundraising. It's actually super helpful for me to hear this, that these are controllable elements of my physical attire or my appearance that might actually just affect the way that people perceive me. And then it gives me this extra hump to get over, in terms of getting to this point of credibility for them to see me as a seasoned operator that I am." She took it so well. But what was interesting about it was actually that she'd made it all this way in her career. She'd even raised funding, and no one had ever given her this feedback. (00:55:21): So this is, I think one of the big challenges of being a woman in Silicon Valley because getting to an executive role or getting to a funded founder role, it's like an Olympic level sport. You have to get all the way through the funnel and become one of the few that are really chosen to do that. But the difficulty of this game is that no one tells you the rules of the game. You actually don't really know what are the rules on how to get intros or give intros. What's the right way to follow up? What are the impressions that people have about you? It turns out that in a career context, it's so unsafe for your manager to turn to a young woman on the team and say, "Here, let me give you feedback on your physical appearance, and how it affects your competence and how you're perceived in the workforce." That the vast majority of them will just never do it because there's no winning, which is similar to the feedback that I got. (00:56:16): SO where I lean in is to say, we're not powerless and there's something that all of us can do if we're in a position where we feel like not even about being female, it's about being perceived as too young or too old, too tall, too short, not the right race. Whatever reason that you feel people may be disqualifying you or not seeing you. We're not powerless, even though this game is rigged. We can study the game, we can help each other, and we can actually start to call out some of those rules and then find ways around them. In this case, for the founder in this example, she really turned to her friends and did a mini makeover and amped up her appearance. (00:57:03): And she came back and she reported, "A lot of people have been giving me really positive feedback, that something about me feels more confident and more energetic, and they can't figure out why." But actually, she was getting a ton of people noticing that something was really different about her in a positive way simply because I was in this great position as her coach to give her some of these pieces of hard feedback that she had never heard before. So it's really on us to try to find those and then try to adapt ourselves to play that game if you want to play at that level.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常微妙的话题。有趣的是，当我试图拆解为什么大家给我那样的反馈时，我觉得很大一部分是——你要尊重作为「非典型」地契合领导岗位或硅谷某些成功职业所带来的内在挑战，承认它。同时也去推动你能掌控的那部分 agency。我先讲一个小故事，关于一个我共事过的人——她授权我在教练语境下分享——然后再退出来。我当时带一位种子期创始人，她特别聪明，非常有活力、非常专注、非常擅长接受反馈并行动。她是那种极优秀的人，我毫不怀疑她会在宇宙中留下巨大印记。(00:52:58)：我们在 Zoom 上合作了几个月，我对她作为 operator 的能力建立了深深的敬意——她思考问题、拆解问题、然后行动的方式。然后我们第一次线下见面吃午饭。我在这里讲都有点紧张。她作为 operator 给我的感觉，和她在这次午饭上最初给我的印象之间的落差，非常 striking——那是个工作日午饭，她穿得像周末在家一样。旧 T 恤、头发用爪夹夹起来、内衣带子露着。在外表上她极其随意。我有点 need to 重新评估，想「哦，这是同一个人，但她呈现出来的样子如此不同」。(00:53:54)：于是见面后，在我们下一次教练 session 里——我们互相邀请对方给反馈——我把这个反馈给了她。我分享了很多我的印象，告诉她：「我尊重你……」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How nervous were you giving her that feedback?
turns.zh: 给她这个反馈时你有多紧张？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: I was so nervous. I actually almost didn't do it, and then took a deep breath and then decided, what the heck? I think she's great. I think she would really benefit from doing it and I gave it. Even in a position where I'm in a relationship with her where I can have that trust, it was super, super difficult. So I can only imagine how hard it is for people to give feedback like that in another context, but how else are people going to hear it?
turns.zh: 我超紧张。我几乎没做，然后深吸一口气，想管他呢，我觉得她很棒，我觉得她会从中受益，然后我就给了。即便在这样一种我们有信任的关系里，也超级、超级难。所以我只能想象在别的场景下给这种反馈有多难，但不然人们怎么听到呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there was a company culture where they talk about how you're being selfish, not giving someone hard feedback because you don't want to be stressed or risk causing damage to your own reputation. But you're not helping them. So it's a really interesting insight of just like, don't be selfish. Do something that's hard when you think it's going to help someone else.
turns.zh: 好像有个公司文化里讲，不给人难听的反馈其实是自私——因为你不想自己有压力或不想冒损害自己声誉的风险。但你没帮他们。所以这是个很有意思的洞察：别自私，做一件难事当你觉得它能帮到别人。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Right. But I think on the topic of being female or on the topic of physical appearance or maybe even some of the topics around being an immigrant, if you're in a position where you can give that feedback, I think the struggle is often will it be well received? And that's where the feedback comes from me from the curiosity loop for this piece, which was there's almost no winning in doing it because the upside is something great happens for them. But there's just so many downsides to giving advice or giving someone input like that the default course is just to avoid. But then that person never learns the rules of the game.
turns.zh: 对。但我觉得在女性这个话题上、在外表这个话题上、甚至移民这个话题上，如果你处在一个能给反馈的位置，挣扎通常在于——它会被好好接收吗？这就是这个话题从好奇心循环里来的反馈——几乎没赢面，因为 upside 是对方因此变好，但给这种建议或 input 的 downside 太多，默认做法就是回避。但那样这个人就永远学不会游戏规则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. It makes me think also a little bit about Radical Candor, basically. I don't know if you read that book, but
turns.zh: 对，完全同意。这也让我想到 Radical Candor。不知道你读过那本书吗？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, Kim Malone Scott, I think.
turns.zh: 读过，Kim Malone Scott，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And Sheryl Sandberg had a similar story where she... I think Sheryl Sandberg gave her a really hard feedback and she didn't take it that well, actually. I think you did a better job, or your friend actually took the feedback and did something with it. I think the whole book was just like, "Hey, I actually do this where people actually listen." I think the framework is, you got to communicate that you care deeply about that person, but you want to challenge them directly also at the same time.
turns.zh: 对。Sheryl Sandberg 也有个类似的故事——我觉得 Sheryl Sandberg 给了她一个很硬的反馈，她当时接受得并不好。我觉得你做得更好，或者你朋友其实接受并行动了。我觉得整本书就是「嘿，我真的这么做而且别人会听」。框架是，你要让对方感受到你深深在乎他，但同时也要直接挑战他。

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great story. I think Sheryl Sandberg took her aside after one of her meetings and basically told her that, "If you say um, it makes me sound stupid." And she didn't take that well, but at the same time, later on in retrospect, she reflected that it was so brave and so helpful of someone like Sheryl to go give that feedback because there's a real cost to it. There's real risk to it.
turns.zh: 对，是个好故事。我觉得 Sheryl Sandberg 在一次会议后把她拉到一边，基本告诉她「你如果说 um，会让我显得很蠢」。她当时没接受得很好，但后来回想，她觉得像 Sheryl 这样的人去给这种反馈是非常勇敢、非常有帮助的，因为它有真实的代价、真实的风险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other thoughts or advice along these lines that you want to leave people with?
turns.zh: 关于这条线你还有什么别的想法或建议想留给大家的吗？

turns.speaker: Ada Chen Rekhi
